t: Inuit, “the people” in Inuktitut and Kalaallisut, descend from the Thule people, who spread east from the Bering Strait around 1000 CE and replaced the Dorset culture, the Tuniit of Inuit tradition.
They lived by hunting whales, seals, caribou and other animals, travelling by qajaq, umiaq and dog sled, and shared food within the household and, to a large extent, the whole community.

Disease, missionaries and Canadian policy, including the High Arctic relocation of the 1950s, transformed Inuit life, but Inuit organised from the 1970s and won land claims, among them the agreement that created Nunavut in 1999.
dyk: A girl of about nine, buried near Utqiaġvik in Alaska around 1200 CE, had been born with a congenital defect and could never walk, yet her family had cared for her all her life.
ev: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, emerge from the Bering Strait and western Alaska and spread east across the Arctic
Inuit migrants reach west Greenland and settle there
Martin Frobisher’s search for the Northwest Passage brings the first well-documented contact between Europeans and Inuit, and he takes three Inuit captive to England
In the High Arctic relocation the Canadian government moves 17 Inuit families from Inukjuak to Resolute and Grise Fiord
Inuit found the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, today Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami
The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement settles the land claim of the Quebec Inuit, with autonomy in the new region of Nunavik
Nunavut is established as a territory of Canada under the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement of 1993

f.homeland: The Arctic and Subarctic north of the tree line: Inuit Nunangat in Canada (Nunavut, Nunavik in northern Quebec, Nunatsiavut in Labrador and the Inuvialuit Settlement Region), Greenland (Kalaallit Nunaat), northern and northwestern Alaska and a few communities on the Chukotka coast of Russia; Greenlandic communities also live in Denmark.
f.period: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, emerge from the Bering Strait and western Alaska around 1000 CE and reach west Greenland by 1100 CE; the Little Ice Age from about 1350; contact with the Norse, then with Martin Frobisher in 1576; settlement and relocation in Canada in the 1950s and 1960s; land claims and self-government from the 1970s to the present.
f.known: the qajaq (kayak) and the umiaq; dog sleds (qamutiik) and the Canadian Inuit Dog; the igloo and the skin tent (tupiq); the inuksuk; women’s face tattoos (kakiniit); carving, printmaking and throat singing; Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit, traditional knowledge and law; the creation of Nunavut in 1999
f.sources: Inuit oral tradition; the Norse sagas; the accounts of William Edward Parry and George Francis Lyon, published in 1824; the work of Franz Boas, Knud Rasmussen and Vilhjalmur Stefansson; archaeology such as the Ukkuqsi site near Utqiaġvik; genetic studies such as one published in Science in 2014; Canadian census figures.
